correctness.rationale: The all-size proof derives exact conditional expectations from the degree-proportional growth rule and the deterministic tree identity sum degree times depth equals twice total depth minus the number of edges. The selected-root indicator times selected-parent depth is identically zero. These facts produce a closed covariance recurrence. Exact mean recurrences, normalization by the root-degree mean, and telescoping give the stated positive-sum formula; summation by parts gives the harmonic closed form. Exact-rational weighted enumeration through size nine independently reproduces the formulas.

originality.rationale: Bibliographic and statement-level comparisons found no theorem matching the exact root-degree/total-root-depth covariance or its size-bias shift. The strongest same-model full source, Feng--Hu, explicitly motivates the connection between large degree and shorter paths but uses topological indices as its bridge. Móri treats maximal degree, and Katona treats degree distributions by level. The closest prior own result couples root degree to leaf count, which does not imply this mixed path-length law.
residual_risks: Older preferential-attachment literature is extensive, and an equivalent formula could appear under the terminology root hub, search cost, Wiener-type depth, or profile.
The Móri and Katona comparisons used their public abstracts and bibliographic material rather than full-paper inspection.
Feng--Hu's motivating average path length is a pairwise-distance statistic, whereas the accepted \(P_n\) is total depth from the distinguished root.

value.rationale: Root degree is the canonical early-hub statistic in the Barabási–Albert tree and total root depth is a canonical global search-cost/profile statistic. The literature explicitly motivates a hub-versus-short-path connection. The accepted identity supplies a direct quantitative bridge: root-degree size bias lowers expected total depth by an exact finite amount asymptotic to (1-log 2)n, and the raw covariance has a nontrivial n^(3/2) scale. This is a structural joint law rather than a routine restatement of marginal moments.
